86	guarded `/api/refresh` endpoint may call Strava.
87	
88	### 3.3 Token handling
89	
90	Refresh tokens rotate, so the live token cannot live in a Worker secret (secrets are
91	read-only at runtime). It lives in KV at `token/refresh`.
92	
93	Rules:
94	
95	1. The new refresh token is written to KV **before** the access token it came with is used
96	   for anything. A crash after that write loses nothing.
97	2. A failed refresh **never** clears or overwrites `snapshot/current`. It writes an error to
98	   `health` only. A stale mood is better than a blank page.
99	3. On a 4xx from the refresh grant, set `health.needsReauth = true`. The page then renders
100	   the last good snapshot plus a reconnect link.
101	4. There is no seed-token secret. Bootstrap and recovery are both the `/auth/login` flow.
102	
103	### 3.4 One-time authorization flow
104	
105	`GET /auth/login?key=<SETUP_KEY>`
106	- Rejects with 404 if the key is absent or wrong (404, not 403, to avoid advertising the route).
107	- Generates a random nonce, stores it at `oauth/state/<nonce>` with a 600-second TTL.
108	- Redirects to `https://www.strava.com/oauth/authorize` with `client_id`, `response_type=code`,
109	  `redirect_uri`, `approval_prompt=auto`, `scope=activity:read_all`, `state=<nonce>`.
110	
111	`GET /auth/callback?code=…&state=…`
112	- Looks up `oauth/state/<nonce>`. Missing or expired -> 400. Deletes it on use, so a state is
113	  single-use.
114	- Exchanges the code (`grant_type=authorization_code`).
115	- Verifies `response.athlete.id === STRAVA_ATHLETE_ID`. Mismatch -> 403, nothing written.
116	- Writes the refresh token to KV, clears `needsReauth`, then immediately runs one refresh so
117	  a snapshot exists within seconds.
118	
119	Both gates matter: the setup key prevents a stranger from starting a flow, and the athlete-ID
120	check prevents a stranger's Strava account from overwriting the owner's token even if they
121	somehow reached the callback.
122	
123	## 4. The mood engine
124	
125	All functions in this section are pure. `now` is always a parameter.
126	
127	### 4.1 Window and fetch
128	
129	90 days of activities via `GET /api/v3/athlete/activities`, with `after` as **epoch seconds**
130	(Strava's unit, not milliseconds), `per_page=200` (Strava's maximum), and at most 2 pages — a
131	hard cap of 400 activities bounds the work. 90 days covers the 12 full weeks the baseline
132	needs.
133	
134	### 4.2 Facts
135	
136	```ts
137	interface Facts {
138	  totalActivities: number          // within the 90-day window
139	  last: LastActivity | null        // name, sportType, distanceM, movingTimeS,
140	                                   // elevationM, startedAt
141	  daysSinceLast: number | null     // fractional days
142	  countLast7: number
143	  countLast14: number
144	  countLast28: number
145	  baselineWeekly: number           // median weekly count, trailing 12 FULL weeks,
146	                                   // excluding the current partial week
147	  streakDays: number
148	  relEffortLast: number            // 0..1
149	  isLongest90: boolean
150	  isFastest90: boolean
151	  previousGapDays: number | null   // days between the last activity and the one before it
152	}
153	```
154	
155	**baselineWeekly.** Median of the per-week activity counts over the 12 full weeks preceding
156	the current partial week. With fewer than 4 full weeks of history, fall back to
157	`countLast28 / 4`. With no history, `0`.
158	
159	**streakDays.** Consecutive calendar days, in a fixed configured IANA timezone (default
160	`America/Los_Angeles`), each containing at least one activity. Counting starts today if today
161	has an activity, otherwise yesterday. If neither has one, the streak is `0`. The timezone is
162	injected, never read from the runtime.
163	
164	**relEffortLast.** Define `effort(a) = a.suffer_score ?? (a.moving_time / 60)`. Compute the
165	percentile rank of the last activity's effort against all *other* activities of the same
166	`sport_type` in the window. Requires at least 5 same-sport samples; otherwise fall back to
167	all sports, which also requires 5; otherwise `0.5`. Percentile rank is
168	`(count of other activities with strictly lower effort) / (count of other activities)`.
169	
170	**isLongest90.** The last activity has the greatest `distance` among same-sport activities in
171	the window, and there are at least 3 prior same-sport samples. The sample floor stops a
172	first-ever activity from registering as a record.
173	
174	**isFastest90.** The last activity has the greatest `average_speed` among same-sport
175	activities in the window whose `distance >= 0.8 * last.distance`, with at least 3 such prior
176	samples. The distance guard prevents a short sprint from beating a long ride.
177	
178	### 4.3 Axes
179	
180	Constants live in `src/domain/tuning.ts`.
181	
182	**Consistency (0–100):**
183	
184	```
185	volumeRatio = countLast7 / max(baselineWeekly, 1)
186	vol         = min(volumeRatio, 1.5) / 1.5           // 0..1, caps at 150% of baseline
187	floor28     = min(countLast28 / 12, 1)              // 12 in 4 weeks = full marks
188	streakPart  = min(streakDays / 5, 1)
189	raw         = 0.55*vol + 0.30*floor28 + 0.15*streakPart
190	recency     = clamp(1 - (daysSinceLast - 3) / 11, 0.15, 1)
191	consistency = round(100 * raw * recency)
192	```
193	
194	`recency` is 1.0 through day 3, then falls linearly to its floor of 0.15 at day 14. With no
195	activities, consistency is `0`.
196	
197	**Charge (0–100):**
198	
199	```
200	charge = round(100 * relEffortLast * 0.5 ** (daysSinceLast / 3))
201	```
202	
203	A 3-day half-life. Effort at the 100th percentile yesterday scores 79; the same effort 9 days
204	ago scores 13. With no activities, charge is `0`.
205	
206	The two axes are deliberately independent: consistency measures showing up over weeks, charge
207	measures how recently hard work happened.
208	
209	### 4.4 Selection
210	
211	Ordered overrides, first match wins. Each returns the mood plus its reason strings.
212	
213	| # | Condition | Mood id |
214	|---|---|---|
215	| 1 | `totalActivities === 0` | `preseason` |
216	| 2 | `daysSinceLast >= 10` | `whered-you-go` |
217	| 3 | `(isLongest90 \|\| isFastest90) && daysSinceLast <= 2` | `believe` |
218	| 4 | `streakDays >= 5` | `roy-kent` |
219	| 5 | `daysSinceLast <= 2 && previousGapDays >= 7` | `comeback-szn` |
220	
221	If none match, select from the score grid. A score of `>= 60` is high; `36–59` is the middle
222	band; `<= 35` is low. The rules below are evaluated in order, so the middle-band rule is
223	checked before the four quadrants.
224	
225	| Condition | Mood id |
226	|---|---|
227	| both scores in 36–59 | `diamond-dogs` |
228	| `consistency >= 60 && charge >= 60` | `football-is-life` |
229	| `consistency >= 60 && charge < 60` | `gaffer-mode` |
230	| `consistency < 60 && charge >= 60` | `hopeful` |
231	| `consistency < 60 && charge < 60` | `biscuits` |
232	
233	Nine moods total.
234	
235	### 4.5 Mood catalogue
236	
237	`src/data/moods.ts`. Data, never logic.
238	
239	```ts
240	interface Mood {
241	  id: string
242	  name: string
243	  accent: string                 // hex, the mood's single ink color
244	  quotes: { text: string; character: string }[]   // 3–5 per mood
245	  gifs: { url: string; alt: string; source: string; verifiedOn: string }[]
246	  verifiedOn: string             // ISO date
247	}
248	```
249	
250	GIF `alt` text is written to read as a complete sentence on its own, so a failed image
251	degrades to a readable caption. A `verifiedOn` older than 180 days renders a staleness marker
252	in the footer.
253	
254	### 4.6 Quote selection
255	
256	```
257	index = fnv1a(String(refreshedAt) + moodId) % quotes.length
258	```
259	
260	Seeded on the snapshot's `refreshedAt`, not the calendar date, so a manual refresh visibly
261	changes the quote even when the mood is unchanged. No `Math.random()` anywhere in the domain;
262	output is a pure function of its inputs and tests assert exact strings.
263	
264	### 4.7 Reasons
265	
266	Every selection emits human-readable reason strings for the receipts block, phrased in terms
267	of observable facts rather than scores. Examples: "4 workouts this week, against your usual
268	2.5", "hardest session in three weeks, and it was yesterday", "9 days since your last
269	activity".
270	
271	**Accuracy rule:** never use the phrase "personal record" or "PR". Activity summaries do not
272	contain best-effort data, so the defensible claim is "longest ride in 90 days".
273	
274	### 4.8 Route geometry
275	
276	`SummaryActivity` already includes `map.summary_polyline` (a Google-encoded polyline, and
277	nullable) plus `start_latlng` / `end_latlng`. This is in the activity-list response we
278	already fetch, so the map costs **zero additional API calls**.
279	
280	The last activity's route is drawn as an inline SVG path in the mood's accent color. There is
281	no base map, no tile provider, no API key, and no client-side JavaScript.
282	
283	The whole pipeline is pure and runs in `src/domain/route.ts`:
284	
285	```
286	decodePolyline(str)      -> LatLng[]        Google polyline algorithm, precision 5
287	privacyTrim(points, m)   -> LatLng[]        drop both ends (see below)
288	simplify(points, eps)    -> LatLng[]        Ramer–Douglas–Peucker, cap ~300 points
289	project(points)          -> XY[]            equirectangular, x scaled by cos(mean latitude)
290	toPath(xy, padding)      -> { pathD, viewBox }
291	```
292	
293	**Privacy trim.** Walk in from the start dropping points until the cumulative haversine
294	distance from the first point exceeds `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` (default 250), then do the same from
295	the end. Routes typically begin and end at the athlete's home, and `activity:read_all`
296	bypasses any Strava privacy zones the athlete has configured — so the untrimmed polyline
297	would reveal more than their public Strava profile does. If fewer than 2 points survive the
298	trim, the route is `null` and the no-route fallback renders instead.
299	
300	**Projection.** Equirectangular with `x = lng * cos(meanLat)` to prevent horizontal
301	squashing, then fit to the viewBox preserving aspect ratio with uniform padding. Web Mercator
302	is unnecessary at the scale of a single activity.
303	
304	**Where trimming happens is load-bearing.** Decode, trim, and simplify all run in the write
305	path. Only the finished `pathD` string reaches `snapshot/current`. Untrimmed coordinates are
306	never persisted in anything the site can serve, which makes the privacy trim a structural
307	property rather than a render-time convention a later change could undo.
308	
309	**No-route fallback.** `summary_polyline` is null for indoor and manually-entered activities
310	(treadmill, gym, manual swim). These render a designed block in the same frame — sport name
311	set large with the duration — never an empty box.
312	
313	**Caption.** Distance, elevation gain, and sport type. Strava's `location_city` /
314	`location_state` are frequently null, so the label renders only when present and its absence
315	changes nothing about the layout.
316	
317	## 5. Storage
318	
319	One KV namespace.
320	
321	| Key | Contents | Notes |
322	|---|---|---|
323	| `token/refresh` | the live rotating refresh token | written before use |
324	| `snapshot/current` | last good `Snapshot` JSON | only written on a fully successful refresh |
325	| `health` | `{ lastAttemptAt, lastSuccessAt, lastError, needsReauth }` | written on every attempt |
326	| `refresh/lastAt` | epoch ms of the last manual refresh | 60s cooldown |
327	| `oauth/state/<nonce>` | pending OAuth state | 600s TTL, single-use |
328	
329	```ts
330	interface Snapshot {
331	  version: 1
332	  refreshedAt: number
333	  mood: { id: string; name: string; accent: string }
334	  quote: { text: string; character: string }
335	  gif: { url: string; alt: string }
336	  scores: { consistency: number; charge: number }
337	  reasons: string[]
338	  facts: PublicFacts
339	  route: {
340	    pathD: string          // already trimmed, simplified, projected
341	    viewBox: string
342	    distanceM: number
343	    elevationM: number
344	    sportType: string
345	    locationLabel: string | null
346	  } | null                 // null for indoor/manual activities, or if the trim consumed it
347	}
348	```
349	
350	Splitting `snapshot/current` from `health` is what makes "a failed refresh never damages the
351	page" structurally true rather than a convention.
352	
353	## 6. Routes
354	
355	| Route | Behavior |
356	|---|---|
357	| `GET /` | Render the page from `snapshot/current` + `health`. Never calls Strava. |
358	| `GET /?preview=<moodId>` | Render any catalogue mood against real stats, with a visible "preview — not your live mood" banner. Ungated; it reveals nothing the page doesn't already show. |
359	| `GET /auth/login?key=` | Setup-key gated. Starts the OAuth flow. |
360	| `GET /auth/callback` | State + athlete-ID gated. Stores the token, runs a first refresh. |
361	| `POST /api/refresh` | Setup-key gated, 60s cooldown. Runs the same orchestration as cron, returns the new snapshot as JSON. |
362	
363	The refresh button renders only when the page is loaded with a valid `?key=`, and the
364	endpoint validates the key independently — it never trusts that the button was present.
365	
366	**Local development:** `wrangler dev --test-scheduled` exposes `/__scheduled`, so the cron
367	handler can be fired by hand with
368	`curl "http://localhost:8787/__scheduled?cron=0+*/4+*+*+*"`. No extra code.
369	
370	## 7. The page
371	
372	Server-rendered HTML with inline CSS. No component framework and no CSS framework, so there
373	are no defaults to accidentally ship.
374	
375	**Visual direction: a non-league matchday programme.** Newsprint stock, heavy condensed
376	display type over a plain text face, one ink accent per mood, hairline rules doing the layout
377	work instead of card shadows, statistics set like a results table. This direction is recorded
378	in `CLAUDE.md` so it is not re-decided each session.
379	
380	Anatomy, top to bottom:
381	
382	1. Thin masthead rule; the mood name set tight and large in the mood's accent.
383	2. The quote — by a wide margin the largest element on the page — with the character's name
384	   beneath in small caps.
385	3. The GIF, beside the quote on wide screens and beneath it on narrow, bordered in the accent.
386	4. The route map: an inline SVG of the last activity's path, stroked in the mood accent on
387	   the newsprint background, in a ruled frame with a caption of distance, elevation, and
388	   sport. No base map, no tiles, no JavaScript. Falls back to the designed no-route block for
389	   indoor and manual activities.
390	5. A hairline rule, then the receipts: last activity name, sport, distance, and when; this
391	   week's count against baseline; streak; days since. Set as a dense tabular block with
392	   lining numerals, deliberately tighter than the hero. That density contrast is the layout.
393	6. Footer: "Powered by Strava" with link-back, the refresh timestamp, the next scheduled run,
394	   and a staleness marker if any displayed GIF's `verifiedOn` is over 180 days old.
395	
396	Manual refresh swaps the quote and GIF in place without a page reload, after a tunable
397	minimum animation duration (default 1200ms) so the change registers as an event. Without
398	JavaScript, the button falls back to a form POST and a redirect.
399	
400	**Designed failure states**, each with real copy:
401	
402	| State | Behavior |
403	|---|---|
404	| No snapshot yet | `preseason` mood, copy stating the first fetch has not run. No fake spinner. |
405	| `needsReauth` | Last good snapshot still renders, plus a reconnect link to `/auth/login`. |
406	| Snapshot older than 12h | Small dated stamp on the masthead. Visible, not alarming. |
407	| No activities in 90 days | `preseason`, with copy that is kind rather than scolding. |
408	| GIF fails to load | Degrades to its `alt` text, which reads as a sentence. |
409	
410	## 8. Testing
411	
412	**Domain — plain Vitest, fixture-driven.** JSON fixtures of Strava responses paired with
413	expected facts, scores, mood, and reasons. Fixtures are ground truth: if the implementation
414	and a fixture disagree, the implementation is wrong. Target at or near 100% branch coverage,
415	gated in CI. Required cases include every override rule, every grid region, and:
416	
417	- an activity exactly 10.0 days old (override 2 boundary)
418	- a first-ever activity, which must not satisfy `isLongest90`
419	- a short fast run that must not satisfy `isFastest90` against longer rides
420	- a DST transition inside a streak
421	- an athlete with under 4 weeks of history (baseline fallback)
422	- zero activities
423	
424	Route geometry (§4.8) gets its own fixture set, since it is the most arithmetic-heavy code in
425	the repo:
426	
427	- `decodePolyline` against the canonical test vectors from Google's polyline documentation
428	- the privacy trim removes at least `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` from **both** ends, verified by
429	  recomputing haversine distance from the original endpoints
430	- an out-and-back route whose start and end are the same point still has both ends trimmed
431	- a route shorter than twice the trim distance yields `route: null`, not a stub path
432	- a null `summary_polyline` yields `route: null` and the no-route fallback
433	- projection preserves aspect ratio, and a route at high latitude is not horizontally stretched
434	- simplification stays under the point cap and never drops the first or last surviving point
435	- a snapshot never contains coordinates outside the trimmed set (asserted directly against
436	  the serialized `pathD`, so a future refactor cannot silently reintroduce them)
437	
438	**Infrastructure — `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` with a mocked Strava.** Required cases:
439	
440	- the rotated refresh token is written to KV before the access token is used
441	- a 4xx refresh leaves `snapshot/current` byte-identical and sets `needsReauth`
442	- a 429 on the activity fetch writes no snapshot
443	- `/api/refresh` rejects a missing or wrong key
444	- `/api/refresh` honors the 60-second cooldown
445	- `/auth/callback` rejects a reused state, an expired state, and a mismatched athlete ID
446	
447	**Render — snapshot tests** over the HTML for all nine moods and every failure state in §7.
448	
449	## 9. Configuration
450	
451	`wrangler.jsonc`: one KV namespace binding, `"crons": ["0 */4 * * *"]`, observability enabled.
452	
453	Secrets: `STRAVA_CLIENT_ID`, `STRAVA_CLIENT_SECRET`, `STRAVA_ATHLETE_ID`, `SETUP_KEY`.
454	
455	Vars: `TIMEZONE` (default `America/Los_Angeles`), `REDIRECT_URI`, `PRIVACY_TRIM_M`
456	(default `250`; set to `0` to disable trimming entirely).
457	
458	## 10. Decisions taken, with the reasoning
459	
460	- **Cron-and-snapshot over lazy revalidation.** Lazy refresh lets data rot when nobody
461	  visits, races between concurrent visitors, and makes page uptime depend on Strava's.
462	- **KV over a Durable Object.** A DO would serialize token writes, but there is exactly one
463	  writer, so KV's consistency model is not a problem worth new infrastructure.
464	- **Curated GIF list over a GIF API.** No API key, no rate limit, no second failure mode, and
465	  no off-topic results. Variety is bounded by curation, which is an acceptable trade.
466	- **Overrides before the grid.** A pure grid cannot express "gone for ten days" or "just set
467	  a 90-day best", which are the most interesting states. A pure rule ladder loses the nuance
468	  of ordinary weeks. Both together cover both.
469	- **No seed-token secret.** Its only job was bootstrap, which `/auth/login` now does better.
470	  Recovery becomes one click instead of a terminal session.
471	- **No OAuth callback for visitors.** Single-athlete by design; the callback exists only for
472	  the owner and is gated twice.
473	- **Inline SVG route over a tile-provider map.** The polyline is already in the data we
474	  fetch, so drawing it ourselves costs nothing: no API key, no per-view request to a third
475	  party, no client-side JavaScript, and no visitor data leaking to a tile host. It is also
476	  fully unit-testable as a pure function, and looks far less generic than an embedded map —
477	  which the project's UI rules require.
478	- **Ghost trails deferred.** Overlaying all 90 days of routes was considered and set aside
479	  for the first build. It needs outlier handling for travel and roughly triples the route
480	  payload. Revisit once the single-route renderer is proven.
481	
482	## 11. Accepted risk, flagged explicitly
483	
484	**The page is public and displays real activity data** — the last activity's name, sport,
485	distance, timing, workout frequency, and the shape of the route. Anyone with the URL can see
486	it. The owner reviewed this on 2026-08-14 and accepted it, and asked for the map specifically.
487	
488	The one mitigation that is **in** the first build is the privacy trim described in §4.8, on
489	by default at 250m. It exists because `activity:read_all` bypasses Strava privacy zones, so
490	an untrimmed route would publish the athlete's home address more precisely than their own
491	Strava profile does. Setting `PRIVACY_TRIM_M=0` disables it; that is a deliberate choice, not
492	a default anyone falls into.
493	
494	Residual exposure after the trim: the general neighborhood, the athlete's training schedule,
495	and any location detail they typed into an activity name themselves. Two further mitigations
496	remain available and cheap if wanted later — a `DETAIL_LEVEL` var that keeps the mood while
497	suppressing the name, route, and exact distance, or putting the whole site behind Cloudflare
498	Access. Neither is in scope for the first build.
499	
500	## 12. Out of scope
501	
502	Mood history and charts (would require D1 rather than a KV snapshot), multi-athlete support,
503	real personal records via per-activity best-effort calls, and webhook-driven near-real-time
504	updates.
505


It must contain, in this order:

1. **What it is** — two sentences, and a note that it is single-athlete.
2. **The one-time setup**, as a numbered list someone can follow without prior knowledge:
   - Create a Strava API application at `https://www.strava.com/settings/api`. Set the Authorization Callback Domain to the Worker's domain (for local work, `localhost`).
   - `npx wrangler kv namespace create STORE`, then paste the returned id into `wrangler.jsonc`.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, rule on the correction, ledger it, and re-dispatch with the ruling carried in the dispatch

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or rule on the load-bearing ones and ledger what you decided. Only
the four classes above stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |

| Tasks | Produces → consumes | Finding |

| Task | Finding |
|---|---|
| 1 | OK. |

### Rulings

Ruling: F1 — Task 2's DST tests assert the wrong days. US DST 2026 begins Mar 8 and ends
Nov 1, so Mar 7→8 and Oct 31→Nov 1 are both ordinary 24-hour days; the 23h and 25h days are
Mar 8→9 and Nov 1→2. The implementation is correct and the tests are wrong. Corrected the
test dates. — Cost if wrong: an implementer would "fix" correct DST code to satisfy a broken
test, breaking streaks twice a year.

Ruling: F2 — spec §4.2 defines `isFastest90` as fastest among activities with
`distance >= 0.8 * last.distance`, and states its purpose is to stop a short sprint beating a
long ride. The formula does not do that: for a 1km sprint, every 10km run passes the filter
and loses on speed. Spec intent is binding; the formula is the argument and it is wrong.
Replaced with a symmetric band — `0.8 * last <= o.distance <= last / 0.8` — so a run is only
compared against comparable distances. Updated the spec, the plan's definition, the tuning
constants, and the implementation. — Cost if wrong: "fastest in 90 days" fires on every short
hard effort, making the `believe` mood meaningless.

Ruling: F3 — Task 12's `deps()` uses `privacyTrimM: 250`, but its fixture polyline is the
3-point continental test vector whose points are ~200km apart; a 250m trim reduces it below 2
points, so `route` is null and the two route assertions fail. The trim itself is thoroughly
tested in Task 8. Gave `deps()` a trim parameter and set the two route tests to 0, which also
strengthens the no-raw-coordinates test by asserting absence while a route is actually
present. — Cost if wrong: Task 12 fails on a fixture artifact and an implementer weakens the
route wiring to compensate.

Ruling: F4 — Task 15 asserts `not.toContain("onerror=")` on escaped output, but escaping
leaves the literal text `onerror="..."` in the document, so the assertion fails
against a correct implementation. Changed it to assert the executable form
`onerror="alert(1)"` is absent while `<img` is present. — Cost if wrong: an implementer
strips characters beyond HTML escaping to satisfy a bad test, mangling legitimate activity
names.

Ruling: F5 — Task 11's `let seen: Request | null = null` assigned inside an async closure
trips TypeScript's control-flow narrowing under `strict`. Switched to a plain
`let seen: Request | undefined` with an explicit cast at the assertion site. — Cost if wrong:
minor; the implementer resolves a type error on its own.

Ruling: F6 — Task 7's `believe` reason renders "and it was just now" for an activity up to 2
days old. Changed to today/yesterday phrasing driven by the same `days` value. — Cost if
wrong: cosmetic only.

Ruling: F7 — Task 9's point-cap test needs `simplifyToCap`, which was module-private. Exported
it and listed it in the task's Produces block. — Cost if wrong: the test cannot compile.

Ruling: F8 — Task 13's interface block omitted `hasSetupKey`, which Tasks 14 and 15 both
import. Added it. — Cost if wrong: two later tasks each invent their own key check, and they
drift.

**Why `privacyTrim` matters and what must not be "simplified".**

This site is public. It renders the shape of the owner's real activities. The app requests the `activity:read_all` Strava scope, which **bypasses any privacy zones the athlete configured on Strava** — so an untrimmed route would publish their home address more precisely than their own Strava profile does. `privacyTrim` is the only thing standing between the route data and that outcome.

<result>## Review: Task 8 — `decodePolyline`, `haversineM`, `privacyTrim` (`src/domain/route.ts`)

### 1. Out-and-back case — derived independently

I hand-traced the test's own fixture: `out = line(100)` (indices 0–99, home→north, ~11.132 m/hop), `back = reversed(out).slice(1)` (99 points, `back[k] = out[98-k]`), `loop = out + back` (199 points, `loop[0] = loop[198] = home`).

Running the actual algorithm: `start` stops at 23 (`23×11.132 ≈ 256 m ≥ 250`), `end` stops at 175 (`loop[175] = out[23]`, same 256 m). Trimmed output runs `out[23] → out[99] (turnaround) → back down to out[23]` — never comes within 250 m of home. Correct and safe.

**But** I also computed what a "cumulative path-length from each end" implementation would do on this *exact* fixture, two natural ways (hop-sum from each end; and single forward-cumulative-from-start with `totalLength − cum(i) ≥ trimM` for the tail). Both land at **the same indices, 23 and 175**, because this fixture has uniform 11.132 m spacing on both legs — index position is a perfect linear proxy for both "distance from home" and "cumulative path length" here. 

**Finding (Important, test-honesty):** the out-and-back test does **not actually discriminate** the straight-line-from-endpoint design from the cumulative-length alternative it's meant to guard against — it passes either way for this fixture. It does still verify something real (trimming works when `first === last` coincide), but it does not prove the safety claim in the doc comment. The implementer's own report hand-traces this and concludes a cumulative implementation would leave points "very close to home" at ~index 175/23 — that's incorrect; index 175/23 is `out[23]`, sitting right at the 250 m boundary, in both approaches. The design rationale in the code comment is still correct in general (see below), just not demonstrated by this specific test.

Where cumulative-vs-straight-line *would* actually diverge: a route that wanders/loops tightly near home for many path-meters before finally moving away in a straight line (e.g., getting the GPS lock in the driveway, circling the block once before heading out) — cumulative-length would burn through `trimM` of path length while still physically near home; straight-line-from-endpoint would not release the trim until physical distance is satisfied. No test exercises this, but it's the real justification for the design — not the fixture given.

### 2. Adversarial cases not covered

- **Loop/lap passing through home mid-route (Critical residual exposure, design limitation not implementation bug):** `privacyTrim` only trims contiguous points from the two array ends. A course that starts away from home, loops past home mid-activity, and continues (e.g., "two laps from the house," or a there-and-back done twice) will have the mid-route home-adjacent points survive untouched in the published output — the two-end slice never scans the interior. Given the stated threat model (bypassing Strava's own privacy zones), this is a genuine way the athlete's home location still leaks through this function, and it's common runner behavior (repeated out-and-backs for mileage). This should be flagged to product/task planning explicitly, even though it's outside this task's literal spec.
- **Uneven spacing / GPS gap at start:** verified fine — the algorithm checks each point's actual distance from the fixed endpoint individually, not a step/index count, so a large gap doesn't cause under- or over-trimming.
- **Asymmetric start-far / end-at-home:** verified fine — `first`/`last` are independent variables, each trimmed against its own reference regardless of which one is actually sensitive. Safe by construction (may over-trim a non-sensitive endpoint, never a safety issue).
- **Antimeridian:** verified safe by trigonometric identity — `sin(θ/2)² = sin((θ+360°)/2)²` because `sin(x+180°) = −sin(x)`, so the un-normalized `dLng` doesn't need explicit wraparound handling. Confirmed numerically (179.9°/-179.9° crossing gives the same `h` as the correct 0.2° short way). Not empirically tested (⚠️ no fixture), but derivation is solid — not a bug.
- **Poles:** formula degenerates gracefully (`cos(lat)→0`), mathematically sound, untested but not a bug.

### 3. `decodePolyline` correctness

Verified against the canonical Google vector (per report) and by inspection: 5-bit chunk accumulation via `(byte & 0x1f) << shift`, continuation via `byte >= 0x20` (matches the `+0x20` OR'd into all non-terminal chunks during encoding), zigzag decode `result & 1 ? ~(result>>1) : result>>1` is the standard formula. Axis order (lat then lng) and cumulative delta accumulation are correct. This is a textbook-correct implementation, not just a test-passing one.

Minor robustness note: on a truncated/malformed input, `charCodeAt` past the string end returns `NaN`; `byte & 0x1f` coerces to 0 and `NaN >= 0x20` is `false`, so the loop terminates rather than hanging or crashing — degrades to a garbage point rather than an infinite loop. Not a privacy issue (Strava's own encoded polylines are well-formed), just worth knowing (Minor).

### 4. Two deliberate behaviours

- **Short route → <2 points:** traced with `line(20)`/`trimM=250`: `start` walks all the way to 20 (array length) since even the last point is only 211.5 m away; `end`-loop then never executes (`end(19) >= start(20)` is false immediately). Result: `slice(20,20)` = `[]`. Confirmed no crash, no negative index.
- **`trimM <= 0` passthrough:** confirmed, returns the same array reference untouched.
- **No partial-trim leakage possible:** proved algebraically — whenever the loops halt due to the distance condition (not array/bound exhaustion), the surviving `start`/`end` points individually satisfy `distance ≥ trimM` from their respective reference. Even in the single-point-remaining edge case, that one point satisfies both endpoint constraints. No state exists where the output looks "trimmed" but a kept point is actually still inside the radius.
- **Downstream caution (Important, out of scope for this task but flag for Task 9):** the function cannot distinguish "caller intentionally disabled trimming" from "config resolved to 0 by accident." If `TUNING.DEFAULT_PRIVACY_TRIM_M` or its plumbing ever resolves to `0`/`undefined→NaN≤0` upstream, this function will silently publish the full untrimmed route including exact home coordinates. Worth an explicit assertion/guard at the Task 9 call site.

### 5. Loop-termination / index safety

Both while-loops are bounds-guarded (`start < points.length`, `end >= start`) and monotonic, so neither can run off the array or invert. Worst case `end` reaches `start - 1`, and `slice(start, end+1)` with `end+1 = start` yields a valid empty slice (never a negative array index). Order is trivially preserved (`slice` is a contiguous sub-range). No bugs found.

### Constants / global-constraint check

`EARTH_RADIUS_M = 6_371_000` is inlined in `route.ts`, not sourced from `src/domain/tuning.ts`, which nominally conflicts with "all constants come from tuning.ts." This is verbatim what the brief itself specified (Step 3), not an implementer deviation. I'd treat it as a defensible exception (it's a physical constant, not a tunable business rule like the rest of `TUNING`), but flagging it since the instruction was stated as absolute (Minor).

No `Date.now()`, no argless `new Date()`, no `Math.random()`, zero imports, no runtime deps — all confirmed by direct read of the file.

### Test honesty summary (12 tests)

11 of 12 tests discriminate a plausible wrong implementation (verified by tracing each: decode sign/shift errors, haversine asymmetry/zero/scale errors, missing start/end/short-route/zero-trim guards would all break their respective test). The exception is **the out-and-back test**, which — as detailed above — passes equally under the cumulative-length alternative it's positioned to rule out, for this specific uniformly-spaced fixture. It still has value (verifies coincident-endpoint handling) but doesn't carry the weight the brief/report assign it.

⚠️ Cannot verify from diff alone: actual coverage percentages and full-suite pass (114/114) — taking the implementer's report as instructed, no internal inconsistency found in the numbers given.

---

### Verdicts

1. **Spec compliance: ✅** — matches the brief's interface and Step 3 code exactly; two deliberate behaviors confirmed; global constraints met except the defensible `EARTH_RADIUS_M` inlining noted above (Minor).

2. **Task quality: approved**, conditional on the following being tracked, not silently dropped:
   - **Critical (design limitation, not a bug in this task):** loop/lap routes revisiting home mid-route are not protected by end-only trimming — needs a decision (accept the risk, require callers to avoid multi-lap publishing, or add mid-route detection in a future task).
   - **Important:** the out-and-back test doesn't actually validate the straight-line-vs-cumulative design claim on this fixture; consider a stronger fixture (non-uniform spacing, or a "wanders near home mid-path" case) in a follow-up, and correct the report's flawed hand-trace if it's referenced later as evidence.
   - **Important:** ensure Task 9's caller can never let `trimM` resolve to `0`/negative by accident.
   - **Minor:** `EARTH_RADIUS_M` literal vs. the "no inlined literals" rule; malformed-polyline degrade-gracefully behavior is untested; antimeridian/pole correctness is derived, not covered by a fixture.

No implementation bugs found in `decodePolyline`, `haversineM`, or `privacyTrim` themselves.</result>

input.old_string:
**Privacy trim.** Walk in from the start dropping points until the cumulative haversine
distance from the first point exceeds `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` (default 250), then do the same from
the end. Routes typically begin and end at the athlete's home, and `activity:read_all`
bypasses any Strava privacy zones the athlete has configured — so the untrimmed polyline
would reveal more than their public Strava profile does. If fewer than 2 points survive the

input.new_string:
**Privacy trim, part one — the ends.** Walk in from the start dropping points until the
**straight-line** haversine distance *from the original first point* exceeds
`PRIVACY_TRIM_M` (default 250), then do the same from the end. Routes typically begin and end
at the athlete's home, and `activity:read_all` bypasses any Strava privacy zones the athlete
has configured — so the untrimmed polyline would reveal more than their public Strava profile
does. If fewer than 2 points survive, the route is `null` and the no-route fallback renders.

The measurement is straight-line distance from the endpoint, **not** cumulative path length
walked. The two diverge exactly where it matters: an athlete who circles the block or waits
for a GPS lock in the driveway accumulates path length while still standing next to the
house, so a cumulative check would release the trim far too early.

**Privacy trim, part two — the middle.** End-trimming alone is not sufficient. A route that
returns past its own start mid-activity — two laps from the front door, or an out-and-back
repeated for mileage, both ordinary training patterns — leaves the athlete's home sitting
in the *interior* of the point list, which a two-ended trim never touches.

So after end-trimming, **drop every remaining point within `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` of either
original endpoint, wherever it appears in the route.** Because this can remove points from
the middle, the result is a list of **segments** (`LatLng[][]`), not one polyline. Segments
shorter than 2 points are discarded; if no segment survives, the route is `null`.

Rendering draws each segment as its own subpath in a single `<path>` element — one `M`
command per segment. The visible result is a route with a gap where the athlete passed home,
which is the correct and honest depiction: it shows where they ran without showing where
they live.

**Redaction happens before persistence, never at render time.** `buildRoute` must also reject
a `trimM` that is not a positive finite number *unless* trimming was explicitly disabled by
configuration — a `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` that silently resolves to `0`, `NaN`, or `undefined`
through a plumbing mistake would publish the full untrimmed route including exact home
coordinates, and that failure must not be quiet.

content.text:
Two findings here you should know about directly, because both concern the thing protecting your address.

**The privacy trim didn't protect lap routes.** It only removes points from the two *ends* of a route. If you run two laps from your front door, or repeat an out-and-back for mileage — ordinary training patterns — your house sits in the middle of the point list, which the trim never touches. All twelve tests passed straight over this, because every one of them only checks the endpoints.

You told me location exposure is acceptable, so I'm not blocking on it. But you were told a 250 m trim exists, and a mitigation should actually do what it says. ---

## The design change: routes are now SEGMENTS, not one polyline

An adversarial review of Task 8 found that `privacyTrim` only removes contiguous points from the two **ends** of a route. A route that passes its own start point mid-activity — two laps from the front door, or an out-and-back repeated for mileage, both ordinary training patterns — leaves the athlete's home sitting in the **interior** of the point list, which end-trimming never touches. This site is public and the app requests `activity:read_all`, which bypasses Strava's own privacy zones, so that is a genuine home-address leak.

The spec (§4.8) now requires a second redaction pass. Implement it:

**1. Add a segment-splitting function.**

```ts
/**
 * Drop every point within `minM` of any reference point, wherever it occurs in
 * the route, and return the surviving runs as separate segments.
 *
 * End-trimming alone cannot protect a lap route that passes its own start
 * mid-activity — the athlete's home survives in the interior. This pass closes
 * that gap. Segments of fewer than 2 points are discarded: a single stranded
 * point is not drawable and is not worth publishing.
 */
export function splitAwayFrom(points: LatLng[], refs: LatLng[], minM: number): LatLng[][]
```

Walk the points once. A point is dropped if it is within `minM` of **any** ref. Each maximal run of kept points becomes a segment. Discard segments with fewer than 2 points.

**2. `buildRoute` composes the full pipeline.** The references are the **original** decoded first and last points, captured *before* `privacyTrim` runs — those are the locations being protected, and they no longer exist in the trimmed array.

```
decode -> capture original first/last -> privacyTrim -> splitAwayFrom(trimmed, [first, last], trimM)
       -> simplifyToCap each segment -> project ALL segments together -> toPath
```

If no segment survives, return `null` and let the caller render the no-route fallback.

**3. Projection must be computed across all segments together.** Every segment shares one bounding box and one scale, or they will not line up with each other. Compute the mean latitude and the extent over the union of all points, then map each segment through the same transform. A per-segment bounding box is a bug that will render as scattered, mutually-inconsistent fragments.

**4. `toPath` emits one subpath per segment** — an `M` command starting each segment, `L` commands within it, all inside a single `d` string. `RouteRender.pathD` stays a `string`, so nothing downstream changes shape. A route with a gap where the athlete passed home is the correct, honest depiction: it shows where they ran without showing where they live.

**5. Guard the trim value.** `buildRoute` must reject a `trimM` that is not a finite number or is negative — throw a clear `Error`. A `PRIVACY_TRIM_M` that resolves to `NaN` or `undefined` through a plumbing mistake would otherwise silently publish the full untrimmed route including exact home coordinates, and that failure must be loud. `trimM === 0` is permitted: it is the documented explicit opt-out, and when it is 0 the redaction pass is skipped entirely (there is no radius to redact).

- All segments share one coordinate system: assert the path's coordinates all fall within the viewBox, and that a two-segment route does not place both segments at the same origin (which is what a per-segment bounding box would produce).
- `buildRoute` throws on `trimM` of `NaN`, `undefined`, and a negative number.
- `trimM === 0` skips redaction and yields a single segment for a route that would otherwise be split.

**10 of 18 tasks committed**, 150 tests passing. Three agents running: reviews for Tasks 9 and 10, plus Task 11 building the Strava client.

Two things I called out explicitly in the Task 11 dispatch, both because they fail *quietly* rather than loudly:

**The `after` parameter is epoch seconds, not milliseconds.** Passing milliseconds doesn't error — Strava cheerfully interprets it as a date roughly fifty thousand years from now and returns an empty list. You'd see "no activities in 90 days" and a Preseason mood, with nothing anywhere indicating a bug. That's the failure mode I'd least like to debug from the outside.

**429 must be checked before the general 4xx branch,** because 429 *is* a 4xx. If the ordering is wrong, hitting a rate limit gets classified as an auth failure, which sets the "needs reauth" flag and puts a "Reconnect Strava" link on your page — telling you to re-authorise over something transient that would have resolved itself in fifteen minutes. The typed errors exist precisely so the refresh orchestration can tell "your token died" apart from "we asked too fast."

The Task 10 review is checking a similar class of quiet bug: whether `getHealth` hands back a *shared* default object rather than a fresh one, where a single caller mutating the result would silently poison every subsequent read.

input.message:
Task 9 fix round 1. Reviewed: spec compliance ✅, quality approved, no Critical issues. The privacy invariant — the entire point of the task — is correctly implemented and is the best-tested property in the file. The reviewer traced it directly: `originalFirst`/`originalLast` are captured before `privacyTrim` runs, and it hand-computed the counterfactual, confirming that had you used the post-trim endpoints as references, the interior HOME point in the lap fixture would sit ~256 m from the wrong reference, survive redaction, and defeat the whole feature. You wired it correctly. It also confirmed the `trimM` guard boundary, per-segment `M` commands with no cross-gap connector, and that `simplifyToCap` cannot reintroduce a redacted point.

**One Important gap to close.**

Nothing tests `buildRoute`'s own decision to project the **flattened union once** rather than per-segment. The existing "shares one bounding box" test calls `project([...clusterA, ...clusterB])` itself and hands already-unified `XY[][]` to `toPath` — so it verifies `toPath`'s bbox math, not `buildRoute`'s composition. The `buildRoute` lap-route test only asserts `M`-count, which is identical either way.

So a future regression changing `project(simplifiedSegments.flat())` to `simplifiedSegments.map(project)` inside `buildRoute` would pass all 27 tests silently, while rendering the route as mutually-inconsistent fragments each normalised to its own origin. Visually it would still be "a route with segments"; it would just be meaningless.

**Add a `buildRoute`-level test** driven through a real encoded polyline, using two widely-separated clusters that both survive redaction. Assert something that is only true under a shared transform — for example, that the two segments' coordinate ranges do **not** both start at the padding origin, and that their relative offset in the output preserves their real-world separation. **11 of 18 complete and reviewed clean.** All remaining briefs are staged.

The build is roughly two-thirds through. What's done: the entire mood engine (facts, both scoring axes, the ten-mood catalogue, selection), route geometry with two-stage privacy redaction, the KV store, and the Strava client. **172 tests**, domain coverage 98.13% against a 95% gate.

What's left: the refresh orchestration (Task 12 — where the token-rotation safety properties actually get exercised), auth and routing, the three page tasks, and setup docs. Plus the deferred GIF pass.

Task 12 is the one I'll watch most closely after the privacy work. It's where the three properties from the spec have to hold simultaneously: the rotated refresh token written to KV *before* the access token it came with is used, a failed refresh leaving the previous snapshot byte-identical, and a 429 not setting the reauth flag. Those are the difference between "the site went stale for four hours" and "you're re-authorising Strava at 11pm because a rate limit got misfiled as a dead token."

Still in flight: Task 9's projection-wiring test and Task 11's review.

## Requirement-by-requirement

**1. `after` is epoch seconds.** `listActivities` interpolates `afterEpochSeconds` straight into the query string (`after=${afterEpochSeconds}`) with no unit math — so whatever unit the caller hands in is what goes out on the wire; this file doesn't introduce a ms bug of its own. The test asserts both `url).toContain("after=1747000000")` **and** `url).not.toContain("1747000000000")`. That second, negative assertion is the one doing real work: a bug that multiplied by 1000 internally would produce `after=1747000000000`, and since that string *contains* `"after=1747000000"` as a prefix, the positive assertion alone would pass anyway — it's the `not.toContain` on the 13-digit form that would actually catch it. Confirmed this is a real check, not a decorative one.

**2. 429 before 4xx.** `assertOk` checks `status === 429` first, `>= 400 && < 500` second. Two dedicated tests (`refresh`, `listActivities`) assert `StravaRateLimitError` specifically on a 429 response — if the branch order were swapped, both would fail because they'd get `StravaAuthError` instead. Correctly pinned.

**3. `suffer_score: 0` — gap found (Important).** The map code is right: `typeof r.suffer_score === "number" ? r.suffer_score : null`, never `||`. But no test in the suite ever passes `suffer_score: 0`. The one relevant test deletes the field (`undefined`), which passes identically whether the code uses `typeof` or `x || null`. So if someone "simplified" this to `r.suffer_score || null` tomorrow, all 20 tests would stay green while a real zero-effort day silently got misclassified as missing data — exactly the corruption the brief warns about. This gap originates in the brief's own verbatim test list (the implementer copied it as instructed, didn't author it), but it's a live hole regardless of whose pen it came from.

**4. `mapActivity` never throws.** Traced every field access: top-level `typeof/null` guard, `start_date` gated by `typeof === "string"` before `Date.parse`, `map` degrades to `{}` for anything that isn't a non-null object, `num()`/`str()` are pure typeof checks. No destructuring, no unguarded property chains. I can't construct an input that throws. Two of the four hostile-input cases the brief names are directly tested (missing `map` object, missing `start_date`); two are not (`start_date` as a number, `map` as a non-object like a string) — implementation handles both correctly via the same generic guards, but there's no test pinning either. Minor.

**5. Pagination bounds.** Loop is `page <= TUNING.MAX_PAGES` (2), breaks when `rows.length < TUNING.PER_PAGE` (200), both sourced from `src/domain/tuning.ts` — no inlined magic numbers. "Stops when short" test (`calls === 1`) would fail if the break were removed. "Stops at the cap" test (`calls === 2` against two full 200-item pages) would fail if the loop bound were removed or raised. Both are real, not tautological. Minor nit: the test hardcodes `2` as a bare literal with a `// MAX_PAGES` comment rather than importing `TUNING.MAX_PAGES` — coupling risk if tuning ever changes, not a correctness issue.

**6. No real network.** Every `new StravaClient(...)` in the test file passes a fake async fetch as the third constructor arg; none fall through to the real-fetch default. Confirmed by inspection, not just report claim.

## Test honesty (20 tests)
Spot-checked the request-inspection tests (`refresh`'s and `listActivities`'s URL/header assertions): both wrap the actual `input`/`init` the client passed into its injected `fetchImpl` in a `new Request(...)` and read back method/url/body/headers from that — they're inspecting the real outgoing call, not a value the test manufactured itself. That's legitimate. Aside from the suffer_score-0 gap above, I didn't find a test that would pass under a plausible wrong implementation.

## Architecture / constraints
- `client.ts`/`map.ts` import only from `../../domain/activity` and `../../domain/tuning` — no `src/app/**` import.
- `src/domain/activity.ts` and `src/domain/tuning.ts` have zero imports — nothing reaching back into infrastructure.
- No new runtime npm dependency introduced.
- `PER_PAGE`/`MAX_PAGES` sourced from `TUNING`, never inlined.
- Diff matches the brief's reference code verbatim — no unrequested additions.

**Spec compliance: ✅.** Every named interface, ordering rule, and epoch-unit contract is implemented as specified, with correct layering and no scope creep.

- **Minor**: `MAX_PAGES` cap test hardcodes `2` instead of importing `TUNING.MAX_PAGES`.

The Task 11 review found something I'd have missed, and it's a good illustration of how a test can create false confidence.

I *did* add a regression test pinning `??`-versus-`||` behaviour for `suffer_score` — back in Task 5. But that test covers `effort()` in the domain layer. The **mapper** has its own, separate `typeof === "number"` check, and nothing tests that one. The existing mapper test deletes the field entirely, which behaves identically whether the code uses a proper type check or a sloppy `||`. So someone could "simplify" the mapper tomorrow, all 20 tests would stay green, and a genuinely easy workout logged with a Strava effort score of zero would get silently reclassified as *missing data* — feeding a neutral 0.5 into the percentile instead of the real zero.

Two places implement the same subtle rule; I only pinned one and assumed I'd covered it. That gap came from my brief's test list, not the implementer.

Also worth noting what the reviewer verified rather than assumed: in the `after=` test, the *negative* assertion is the one doing the work. A bug multiplying by 1000 produces `after=1747000000000`, which still **contains** `after=1747000000` as a prefix — so the positive assertion passes against the broken code. Only the check for the absence of the 13-digit form catches it.

That fix is queued rather than dispatched. Task 9's fix round is still live, and I said I'd run one implementer at a time after the earlier concurrency slip — so I'm waiting rather than quietly relaxing the rule I just set.

1. **The rotated refresh token is written to KV *before* the access token it came with is used for anything.** Strava rotates the refresh token on every use and invalidates the old one.
